extracted.intended_audience: writers, critics, and students learning to distinguish parody, satire, and pastiche (humor/literary study)
extracted.subtask_description: A short rubric for identifying and distinguishing parody, satire, and pastiche by asking about target, tone, degree of transformation, agenda for change, and required audience knowledge of the original work.

rubrics_metrics.name: What is being targeted
rubrics_metrics.description: Determine whether the piece targets a specific work, a genre/style, or the real world/society.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use the side-by-side distinctions: satire targets the real world or society (vice, folly, abuse, especially those in power); parody targets a specific work or genre (attacks style/content of a fictional work to reveal its ridiculousness); pastiche targets a style and imitates it (often as homage). Examples: 'A Modest Proposal' targets societal behavior (satire); 'Spaceballs' targets Star Wars (parody); 'The Hours' emulates Virginia Woolf's style (pastiche).

rubrics_metrics.name: Tone
rubrics_metrics.description: Assess the tone of the piece (angry, playful, affectionate).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Match tone to genre: satire is often angry or venomous and seeks to attack or change; parody is generally gentler, playful, and can be good-natured or affectionate while still critiquing; pastiche is affectionate or admiring and lacks mockery. Tone helps distinguish intent — biting anger suggests satire, playful mimicry suggests parody, admiration suggests pastiche.

rubrics_metrics.name: Transformative vs. imitative
rubrics_metrics.description: Decide whether the work transforms its source for commentary or simply imitates its style.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Parody is transformative: it adopts the attacked work's guise to reveal inherent ridiculousness (uses imitation as a vehicle for critique). Pastiche is imitative and not transformative — it emulates distinctive qualities out of admiration without mockery. Satire can use transformation or original modes but is defined by its critical aim, not necessarily by mimicry. Consider whether the imitation adds critical perspective (transformative) or merely reproduces style (imitative).

rubrics_metrics.name: Does it have an agenda for change
rubrics_metrics.description: Determine whether the piece seeks to provoke change or simply comment/entertain.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Satire typically has an explicit agenda: it uses humor to criticize vice and aims to inspire reform or destruction of what it attacks. Parody usually aims to critique or expose flaws in a work or genre but not to change society broadly; it is often playful rather than reformist. Pastiche generally lacks an agenda for change and functions as homage or celebration.

rubrics_metrics.name: Does the audience need to know the original
rubrics_metrics.description: Evaluate whether appreciation depends on familiarity with the source work or style.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Parody and pastiche often rely on the audience recognizing the original work or style to get the joke or homage — parody uses resemblance to highlight flaws, pastiche evokes a recognizable style as tribute. Satire can target societal issues and may not require knowledge of a specific original; its punch relies on recognizing the social target rather than a particular source text. Consider how much background knowledge is needed for the piece's humor or critique to land.
